title: Making peace with your story
hook: finding God even in the chapters you'd delete

segments.voice: Yesterday, courage: Joshua told be strong and of a good courage, and Esther saying if I perish, I perish. Your line was brave enough. Did you take the first step you chose? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

If your life were a book, which chapter would you tear out? The year everything fell apart. The thing you did, or the thing that was done to you. The friendship that ended badly. Some people carry a page like that, folded small, kept out of sight. The Bible has a man whose life is full of chapters he'd have every right to tear out: thrown in a pit by his own brothers, sold as a slave, falsely accused, forgotten in prison. And at the end of his story he says something about those chapters to the very brothers who wrote them. Today: making peace with your story.

The man is Joseph, in Genesis. His brothers, jealous, strip off his coat, throw him in a pit, and sell him to traders headed for Egypt. There he's a slave, then accused of a crime he didn't commit, then left in prison. Years later he rises to run Egypt's grain stores, and in a famine his brothers come to buy grain, not knowing who he is. There is a reunion, with tears. But the scene that matters today comes later, after their father Jacob dies. The brothers panic. Now, they think, Joseph will finally pay us back. They send word asking to be forgiven, and Joseph weeps. Then they come and fall down before him. Then he says, in the King James words: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God? But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." Listen to how careful that is. Joseph doesn't say the pit was good. He doesn't say what they did was fine. He calls it evil, plainly. But he says God was at work in the same chapter, bending it toward saving lives. Both things are true at once. That's what making peace with your story looks like here. Not pretending a hard chapter didn't happen. Not tearing it out either. Letting God hold it. The prophet Joel, after locusts have stripped the land, hears God promise his people: "I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten." And a psalm says even the dark chapters are not hidden: "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." Christians explain how God works in suffering in different ways, and some are wary of easy answers. But Joseph's story offers this much: in Genesis, even the pit is inside the story God is telling.
screen: `YE THOUGHT EVIL; GOD MEANT IT UNTO GOOD.`
`THE DARKNESS AND THE LIGHT ARE ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a hard chapter with grace. Settle, and breathe. Choose one chapter of your life you'd rather delete. Not the very worst, if that's too much today; one you can look at. Let yourself see it plainly, the way Joseph named it evil. Then ask, gently: is there anything that grew in me, or around me, after it? A strength, a friend, a kindness I now have for others? You don't have to find one. If you pray, you can bring the chapter to God with Joel's line, I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten, and leave it there for the sit. The bell holds the time.
Making peace with your story. In Joseph's words, naming the evil honestly, and trusting that God was at work in the same chapter.
screen: `MAKING PEACE WITH YOUR STORY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: every chapter held. Today, when that hard chapter comes to mind, don't slam the book. Say to yourself, this too is held, and turn the page. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Christians bring the hard parts of their lives to God in prayer, confession, counseling and spiritual direction, and some practice a prayerful review of the day or of their life, looking for where God was present.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your father has died, and the brothers who sold you into slavery are on their knees, afraid you'll finally pay them back. what do you do?
options: take your revenge now that your father is gone.
weep, tell them fear not, and promise to care for them.
send them away and never see them again.
fork.reveal: Joseph weeps and says, fear not: for am I in the place of God? ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. then he promises to nourish them and their little ones.

trapdoor: what you thought: making peace with your past means pretending it was fine.
what it means: Joseph names the evil plainly and still sees God at work in the same chapter.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 50:20 holds two intentions over one event: the brothers meant evil, God meant good. the text doesn't cancel either one.
